title: Smith et al. (2007): Short-answer practice
instructions: Answer in English with a concise concept or phrase. Interpret the interview accounts and study methods; you do not need to memorize participants' names.

items.question: What concept describes a culturally dominant, traditional patriarchal ideal of manliness?
items.explanation: The article discusses expectations such as toughness, control, and independence. It also acknowledges that masculinities vary across cultures and settings, rather than treating one ideal as every man's identity.

items.question: Which two qualities does the dominant masculine definition of independence privilege?
items.explanation: These qualities can shape help-seeking expectations. The authors compare this meaning of independence with maintaining daily functioning and quality of life as people age.

items.question: Which aging discourse treats the ability to remain independent as a marker of doing well in later life?
items.explanation: The article examines how this discourse overlaps with masculinity. Independence can carry health-enhancing as well as health-damaging meanings, depending on how it is understood and enacted.

items.question: Which broader men's health study supplied participants for the qualitative sub-study in North-West Adelaide?
items.explanation: The full cohort contained 1,195 men aged 35–80. The qualitative sub-study involved 36 men, and this paper primarily drew on the older participants' understandings. The full cohort is not the interview sample.

items.question: Which two characteristics were used to stratify invitations to the qualitative sub-study?
items.explanation: The researchers invited 36 men using these strata. The table includes 22 men in the 55+ age categories, including 12 aged 65 or older; the paper does not represent a population-wide experiment.

items.question: Which interview format combined core questions with flexible, open-ended follow-up discussion?
items.explanation: Four pilot interviews informed the core questions and probes. The flexible format let participants guide discussion while maintaining coverage of help seeking and health-service use.

items.question: Which analytic approach developed themes from the interview material?
items.explanation: The primary researcher transcribed the interviews, included field notes where needed, and used NVIVO for coding. The software supported the analysis; its name is not the analytic method.

items.question: What interactional process helped participants speak openly about sensitive or stigmatized health concerns?
items.explanation: Shared experiences and discussion of family, hobbies, and life histories helped create a setting for disclosure. The findings challenge an assumption that men are invariably unwilling to discuss health.

items.question: In the diabetes account, which aspect of independence was expressed by wanting to manage the illness rather than be ruled by it?
items.explanation: The participant framed illness management through being in control. The authors connect such language with masculine identity while examining how independence also relates to aging and quality of life.

items.question: What concern did the man who declined to call his lodger after a fall express about asking for assistance?
items.explanation: The account describes reluctance to place demands on others even when help was available. It illustrates one possible harmful consequence of interpreting independence as avoiding reliance on others.

items.question: Which two social positions did Max's account bring together when he defended continuing to care for himself?
accepted_answers: being a man and growing older
items.explanation: His account combined masculine independence with concern about losing a longstanding independent way of life as he aged. The authors argue that describing him only as stubborn misses this overlap.

items.question: Which two dimensions of functioning did an interviewee explicitly connect with being able to live independently?
items.explanation: The section includes middle-aged participants David and Bob as well as older men. Their accounts link independence with everyday capacities and a full life, rather than longevity alone.

items.question: Which sensory capacity did one participant link to continuing to read and drive?
items.explanation: His concern was how losing this capacity could undermine daily activities and quality of life. The example illustrates the meaning of a specific limitation, not a universal response to sensory loss.

items.question: Which aspect of living did the account of losing a driving licence prioritize over merely surviving?
items.explanation: The participant described reduced mobility, remoteness, and distress after losing his licence. The authors use the account to examine the value attached to meaningful daily life; it is not a general evaluation of lives with disability.

items.question: What mobility aid enabled a participant with limited walking ability to visit local shops and his doctor independently?
items.explanation: The aid allowed independence to take a new form through supported mobility. The authors interpret this as a reformulation of idealized masculinity and daily independence, rather than equating independence with refusing every form of support.
